title: How Upfront Work Makes Healthcare Migration More Predictable
summary: Assessment, dependency mapping, governance and repeatable migration planning give healthcare teams a clearer, more controlled path from discovery through execution.
body_markdown:
In a large infrastructure transformation, migration day usually gets most of the attention. The predictability of that day, however, is shaped much earlier. In healthcare, that upfront work carries added weight because applications, infrastructure and operating processes are closely connected, and avoidable disruption can affect critical clinical and business operations. For the migration to succeed, teams need to understand in detail how the environment works, which systems depend on one another, who can make decisions when conditions change, how each move will be tested and what happens if validation fails.


In my experience, clarity on those points is a major factor in migration predictability. Healthcare environments can span thousands of workloads and hundreds of applications, supported by databases, storage, networking, security and disaster recovery. When we migrate workloads into Rackspace Clinical First Cloud™, that dependency picture informs sequencing, testing and recovery planning.


At that scale, the unit of planning is rarely an individual workload. Applications often rely on shared infrastructure and services, so migration waves need to reflect those relationships rather than treat each workload as an isolated move.


### Start with the environment as it works today


Assessment is a major part of these engagements. Building an inventory of applications, workloads and supporting infrastructure gives us a baseline view of the environment, but the work goes beyond identifying what’s there.


Automated discovery and dependency mapping show us which applications need to move together, what they depend on across network, storage and database environments, and what their recovery requirements are. We then validate that information through technical workshops and conversations with the teams closest to the applications and infrastructure.


From there, we can group workloads around those relationships and build migration waves with a clearer view of what needs to be ready, which teams need to participate and how each application will be validated after the move.


### Add strong governance to help migration teams move faster


Governance can feel like one more layer of process. However, in a large migration, clear governance can actually help teams move faster. Clear decision rights, defined ownership and established escalation paths help teams respond quickly when conditions change without losing time determining who needs to make the call.


Large migrations require decisions throughout planning and EXECution. Dependencies can change, workloads may not be ready when expected, capacity may need to be adjusted and testing can uncover issues that need to be resolved before work continues.


We start by making roles and accountability clear across the program, then build in regular program- and project-level reviews to manage risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies. Escalation paths, formal change control and EXECutive oversight through a steering committee give teams a clear way to handle decisions that need broader alignment.


When conditions change, teams know who owns the decision, who needs to be involved and when escalation is required. That clarity helps technical teams stay focused on EXECution while program leaders manage change consistently across the migration.


### Build a repeatable migration motion


Once the environment is understood and the governance structure is in place, we can organize the migration around a repeatable process. That includes defined migration waves, detailed runbooks, testing plans, go/no-go criteria, communications and rollback plans.


The process stays consistent while still accounting for application-specific requirements. Each wave starts with clear prerequisites, sequencing, owners, validation steps, decision points and fallback procedures. The team knows what needs to happen before the move, how the application will be validated afterward and what to do if the result does not match the plan.


As the migration progresses, lessons from one wave can inform the next. Teams can refine how they plan, communicate, validate and respond without reinventing the process for every application. That also makes risk easier to identify and manage before each migration window.


### Account for continuity in each migration wave


Continuity planning should be part of every migration from the start. Applications, infrastructure services and operating processes still need to function as expected while the environment changes.


Dependency mapping, governance, testing and rollback planning all support that continuity. A workload can move successfully and still create downstream problems if a connected service, dependency or validation requirement has been missed. For each migration wave, teams need a clear view of what must be ready, what must be tested, who can make decisions and what happens if validation does not go as planned.


### Treat pre-migration work as part of delivery


Assessment, governance and migration design are part of the migration itself. Assessment gives teams a clear view of the environment. Governance defines how decisions are made and escalated. Migration planning puts that understanding into practice through defined waves, runbooks, testing and rollback procedures. Together, that work makes EXECution more predictable.


At Rackspace, we support customers from assessment through ongoing operations. We help them understand the current environment, decide how workloads should move, build the target platform, EXECute the migration and operate the environment over time. That level of coordination becomes especially important when thousands of workloads and hundreds of applications have to move in groups according to technical and business dependencies.


By the time a migration wave begins, the environment should be mapped, responsibilities clear and validation plans defined. That keeps the migration window focused on EXECution rather than discovery or decisions that should have been addressed earlier.
